citations.quote: | A-ST20-SRVT-HI | ST20 Weld cell A: servo temperature high | `servo_temp_c` above 72 degC; alarm: the station keeps running |

Servo-gun drive temperature (`servo_temp_c`) rises above its normal range of 35 to 65 degC. Above 66 degC the drive derates its speed, adding about 0.8 s to the cycle for every degree above that point, so the cell cycle time rises and stations downstream are starved. The 72 degC alarm comes before the 80 degC trip. A failing cabinet fan is often audible before the trip.
On ST30, check coolant flow first: a servo temperature rise that follows a fall in coolant flow is a cooling-circuit problem (see Section 6.4), not a drive problem.

| `servo_temp_c` above 65 degC, cycle time normal | Cabinet fan failing or filter mat clogged; high ambient temperature | Listen to the cabinet fan; inspect the filter mat; compare cabinet and ambient temperature | Clean or replace the filter mat; replace the fan (see Table 7-1) |

citations.quote: Typical signature. Coolant flow (coolant_flow_lpm, ST30 only) falls below its normal range of 10 to 14 L/min and the 8 L/min low alarm follows. With less cooling, servo temperature starts to rise about 15 minutes later, then the drive derates (cycle time rises) and finally trips on over-temperature. Weld current becomes noisier as the electrodes run hot.
Falling coolant flow followed some minutes later by rising servo temperature identifies a restricted coolant circuit; a servo temperature rise without any flow change does not.
Coolant flow that falls at ST30 while the chiller supply temperature stays normal points to a restriction inside the cell (strainer, kinked hose, scaled gun passages), not to the chiller.
| coolant_flow_lpm below 10 L/min | Cell strainer clogged | Read the strainer differential gauge; inspect the strainer basket | Clean the strainer basket under energy control (Chapter 8) |

citations.quote: When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows. The weld cells see their regulated gun air fall shortly after; gun force alarms follow, and when gun air reaches each cell's own low limit (see the weld cell manual) the supply-air interlock stops that cell. A leak is often audible as a hiss at the leak point.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.

| Header pressure falling, compressor loaded continuously | Distribution leak (drop legs, couplings, hoses) or a new air user | Ultrasonic leak survey of the header and the ST20/ST30 drop legs with the cells stopped | Repair the leaks; confirm the header holds pressure (see Table 3-2) |

citations.quote: In normal service the compressor loads at 6.2 bar and unloads at 7.3 bar, so header pressure (`header_pressure_bar`) saw-tooths inside its normal range of 6 to 7.5 bar and motor current (`compressor_current_a`) switches between about 92 A loaded and about 38 A unloaded, a load/unload cycle of roughly 2 minutes. A leak first shows as a longer loaded time: average motor current rises while header pressure still recovers. When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.

| Header pressure falling, compressor loaded continuously | Distribution leak (drop legs, couplings, hoses) or a new air user | Ultrasonic leak survey of the header and the ST20/ST30 drop legs with the cells stopped | Repair the leaks; confirm the header holds pressure (see Table 3-2) |

| Header pressure low, compressor current low (not loading) | Inlet valve stuck closed, or load control fault | Check the compressor display for load status and faults | Repair the inlet valve or load control |

citations.quote: Regulated gun air (`air_pressure_bar`) normally sits at 5.6 bar within 5.3 to 5.9 bar. Below 5 bar the cell raises a low-air alarm; at 4.6 bar the supply-air interlock stops the cell. Gun force alarms (A-ST20-GUN-FRC, A-ST30-GUN-FRC) can appear as the air falls.

When gun air pressure falls at ST20 and ST30 together, the cause is upstream in the plant air supply; check the header pressure (see Section 6.2 of AM-CA-01 (Plant Air System and Utilities)) before working on either cell.
When gun air falls at one cell only, check that cell's filter-regulator, drop-leg ball valve and quick couplings.

| Gun air low at one cell only | Filter-regulator element clogged, regulator drifted, or local leak | Read the cell gauge; listen for leaks at the drop leg and couplings | Replace the filter element; reset the regulator; repair the leak |

Tip resistance (`tip_resistance_mohm`) climbs steadily over hours from about 0.15 mOhm towards the 0.185 mOhm alarm limit as the tip faces pick up coating material and oxide (which raises contact resistance) and lose their shape, while the current stepper raises weld current (`weld_current_ka`) to compensate. citations.quote: In normal service the compressor loads at 6.2 bar and unloads at 7.3 bar, so header pressure (`header_pressure_bar`) saw-tooths inside its normal range of 6 to 7.5 bar and motor current (`compressor_current_a`) switches between about 92 A loaded and about 38 A unloaded, a load/unload cycle of roughly 2 minutes. A leak first shows as a longer loaded time: average motor current rises while header pressure still recovers. When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.

| Header pressure falling, compressor loaded continuously | Distribution leak (drop legs, couplings, hoses) or a new air user | Ultrasonic leak survey of the header and the ST20/ST30 drop legs with the cells stopped | Repair the leaks; confirm the header holds pressure (see Table 3-2) |

| Header pressure low, compressor current low (not loading) | Inlet valve stuck closed, or load control fault | Check the compressor display for load status and faults | Repair the inlet valve or load control |

citations.quote: Tip resistance that rises in a straight line over several hours, together with a stepping weld current, is the signature of electrode tip wear, not of a controller fault.

Tip resistance (`tip_resistance_mohm`) climbs steadily over hours from about 0.15 mOhm towards the 0.185 mOhm alarm limit as the tip faces pick up coating material and oxide (which raises contact resistance) and lose their shape, while the current stepper raises weld current (`weld_current_ka`) to compensate. Rejects at ST60 follow later, once the weld nuggets become undersized. Servo temperature, gun air pressure and cycle time stay normal.

Tip resistance (`tip_resistance_mohm`) climbs steadily over hours from about 0.15 mOhm towards the 0.185 mOhm alarm limit as the tip faces pick up coating material and oxide (which raises contact resistance) and lose their shape, while the current stepper raises weld current (`weld_current_ka`) to compensate. Tip resistance that rises in a straight line over several hours, together with a stepping weld current, is the signature of electrode tip wear, not of a controller fault.

citations.quote: When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows. The weld cells see their regulated gun air fall shortly after; gun force alarms follow, and when gun air reaches each cell's own low limit (see the weld cell manual) the supply-air interlock stops that cell. A leak is often audible as a hiss at the leak point.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.
A fall in gun air pressure at ST20 and ST30 at the same time, after the header pressure has fallen, places the cause in the air supply, not in the weld cells.

| Header pressure falling, compressor loaded continuously | Distribution leak (drop legs, couplings, hoses) or a new air user | Ultrasonic leak survey of the header and the ST20/ST30 drop legs with the cells stopped | Repair the leaks; confirm the header holds pressure (see Table 3-2) |

citations.quote: Regulated gun air (`air_pressure_bar`) normally sits at 5.6 bar within 5.3 to 5.9 bar. Below 5 bar the cell raises a low-air alarm; at 4.6 bar the supply-air interlock stops the cell. Gun force alarms (A-ST20-GUN-FRC, A-ST30-GUN-FRC) can appear as the air falls.

When gun air pressure falls at ST20 and ST30 together, the cause is upstream in the plant air supply; check the header pressure (see Section 6.2 of AM-CA-01 (Plant Air System and Utilities)) before working on either cell.
When gun air falls at one cell only, check that cell's filter-regulator, drop-leg ball valve and quick couplings.

| Gun air low at one cell only | Filter-regulator element clogged, regulator drifted, or local leak | Read the cell gauge; listen for leaks at the drop leg and couplings | Replace the filter element; reset the regulator; repair the leak |

citations.quote: Outlet pressure (`pump_pressure_bar`) starts to pulse at the pump stroke rate (0.15 Hz, one stroke about every 6.7 s) and its mean falls. The bead becomes narrow and uneven (A-ST40-BEAD-QA) and ST60 rejects rise.
Insufficient volume at the dispense nozzle causes the applied bead width to shrink, triggering alarm A-ST40-BEAD-QA and raising downstream part reject counts at ST60.
Bead width (`bead_width_mm`) normally stays within 3.6 to 4.4 mm. The 3.4 mm and 4.6 mm limits raise A-ST40-BEAD-QA.
A narrow bead with normal flow and pressure points to the nozzle or the bead program; a narrow bead with low flow points to the pump supply (see Section 6.2).

citations.quote: Typical signature. Coolant flow (coolant_flow_lpm, ST30 only) falls below its normal range of 10 to 14 L/min and the 8 L/min low alarm follows. With less cooling, servo temperature starts to rise about 15 minutes later, then the drive derates (cycle time rises) and finally trips on over-temperature. Weld current becomes noisier as the electrodes run hot.
Falling coolant flow followed some minutes later by rising servo temperature identifies a restricted coolant circuit; a servo temperature rise without any flow change does not.
On ST30, check coolant flow first: a servo temperature rise that follows a fall in coolant flow is a cooling-circuit problem (see Section 6.4), not a drive problem.

citations.quote: In normal service the compressor loads at 6.2 bar and unloads at 7.3 bar, so header pressure (`header_pressure_bar`) saw-tooths inside its normal range of 6 to 7.5 bar and motor current (`compressor_current_a`) switches between about 92 A loaded and about 38 A unloaded, a load/unload cycle of roughly 2 minutes. A leak first shows as a longer loaded time: average motor current rises while header pressure still recovers. When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.
A header pressure reading that falls while compressor duty and the gun air pressures at both cells stay normal points to the header pressure transmitter; see Section 6.4.

| Header pressure falling, compressor loaded continuously | Distribution leak (drop legs, couplings, hoses) or a new air user | Ultrasonic leak survey of the header and the ST20/ST30 drop legs with the cells stopped | Repair the leaks; confirm the header holds pressure (see Table 3-2) |

citations.quote: Regulated gun air (`air_pressure_bar`) normally sits at 5.6 bar within 5.3 to 5.9 bar. Below 5 bar the cell raises a low-air alarm; at 4.6 bar the supply-air interlock stops the cell. Gun force alarms (A-ST20-GUN-FRC, A-ST30-GUN-FRC) can appear as the air falls.

When gun air pressure falls at ST20 and ST30 together, the cause is upstream in the plant air supply; check the header pressure (see Section 6.2 of AM-CA-01 (Plant Air System and Utilities)) before working on either cell.
When gun air falls at one cell only, check that cell's filter-regulator, drop-leg ball valve and quick couplings.
| Gun air low at both ST20 and ST30 | Plant air header pressure low (leak or compressor problem) | Check `header_pressure_bar` on UT-AIR | Follow the plant air and utilities manual, Section 6 |

Servo-gun drive temperature (`servo_temp_c`) rises above its normal range of 35 to 65 degC. Above 66 degC the drive derates its speed, adding about 0.8 s to the cycle for every degree above that point, so the cell cycle time rises and stations downstream are starved. This derating penalty adds 0.8 s to cycle duration for every degree Celsius above 66 degC. As speed falls, cell cycle time rises past the nominal 50 s standard, causing downstream starvation. If temperature reaches 72 degC, the cell issues an over-temperature alarm, followed by a total cell trip at 80 degC. An audible cabinet fan problem often precedes the trip.
